newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals - Business slow amid summer doldrums.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals - Business slow amid summer doldrums.

text.p: Scant trader business and a lack of buying from consumers basking in the traditional summer lull saw most minor metals wilt over the last week, traders said on Thursday.
Cobalt slipped under pricing, antimony probed lower and was eyeing levels towards $2,000 a tonne, while bismuth after recent gains moved into consolidation.

"Overall the market has turned quiet with prices drifting lower mostly under a lack of interest," one trader said. "It's the time of year when you start signing off fewer contracts," another commented.
On cobalt one trader added, "Russian cobalt has recently been talked down in order to give people an extremely good buying opportunity."
The trader believed the market remained tight and expected prices to rally in August towards $30 a pound against a backdrop of low stocks.
The trader said that consumption of cobalt was increasing and is expected to reach 28,500 tonnes in 1997. He estimated that total stocks held by major producers was roughly below 1,500 tonnes.
Other traders suggested that there was enough material to meet current demand.
News that Congo's state mining company Gecamines has a two-month stockpile of around 670 tonnes of metal was noted.
Gecamines chairman Mbaka Kawaya said in an interview in Mauritius that the company would air freight cobalt which had already been sold.

One London based trader said that the delivery of material into Europe could add to pressure on prices that have recently been easing against the backdrop of pricing operations and a slowing in consumer demand.
"There are enough units on the ground in Europe to meet demand ...there may be some easing in the price but I believe it is close to bottoming out," this trader said.

But a source with close contacts in the Democratic Republic of the Congo expressed doubt on the figure of 670 tonnes as he believed that it was a projection of 1996 figures. According to this source the amount that Gecamines holds now is around 200 tonnes of off grade material.
Antimony drifted under Chinese offers as they attempted to book profits before the summer lull takes a firm grip. Traders opinions on antimony's next direction were divided.
Several believed that the $2,000 barrier could easily be eroded over the coming weeks as consumers started to live from hand to mouth before replenishing stocks when activity picks up later in 1997.
"They (consumers) will not have to cover until late August/early September," one trader said.

But others believed that the market would soon bounce back with aggression. Comparing antimony to a piece of over extended elastic one trader said, "It has been stretched to far on the downside. The market is likely to turn and snap back up in our faces."
The trader said he expected fresh buying and covering towards $2,000.
Bismuth calmed and looked to be moving into a period of consolidation below $4.00 a pound.

Traders said material was still thin on the ground but several believed prices would not breach $4.00 a pound near-term. "Overall the market is still going up but at the moment it is in a state of limbo," one said.
Elsewhere, magnesium moved higher on increased demand, while the recent gains in platinum group metal rhodium slowed as palladium eased back from recent 17 year highs of $240.00 an ounce.
